system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2119-07-13 20:48:00 to 2119-07-14 18:33:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted due to malfunction of her hemodialysis catheter, which failed despite initial replacement and tPA treatment. A new tunneled catheter was successfully placed, restoring dialysis access. During admission, she was found to have infected calciphylaxis wounds with polymicrobial growth including Pseudomonas, prompting a 10-day course of ciprofloxacin and clindamycin. Her severe hyperparathyroidism (PTH 1110) was confirmed as a driver of calciphylaxis, and she was scheduled for surgical evaluation for parathyroidectomy. Left heel pain was evaluated with X-ray, showing no fracture but findings consistent with plantar fasciitis. She was discharged to an extended care facility on antibiotics and with wound care instructions, to continue dialysis and follow up with surgery.
problems: Mechanical complication of other vascular device, implant, and graft
Pseudomonas infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of worsening pain in your skin wounds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. The pain in my left hip, right breast, and belly got much worse during dialysis. It’s sharp and comes and goes, but it’s worse at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve been dealing with calciphylaxis for a while. The ER team started you on IV antibiotics—clindamycin and cipro—because there’s concern for infection in the wound areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that same infection last month. They gave me antibiotics then. Is it back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The gram stain from your thigh ulcer showed a small amount of bacteria, mostly white blood cells and some gram-positive cocci. It’s not a heavy infection, but we’re treating it to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But the pain is mostly from the calciphylaxis, not just infection, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The calciphylaxis is the main issue—those chalky, firm areas on your skin are calcium deposits. They’re very painful. Dermatology recommends trying intralesional sodium thiosulfate injections once you’re out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t tolerate the IV version before—made me vomit. Are the shots better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, these are injections directly into the wounds. They’re usually better tolerated and can help heal the lesions and reduce pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m willing to try. Anything to stop this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your white count is coming down—from 12.6 to 10.9—so the antibiotics are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Is my kidney function okay? I’m worried about that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is up a bit to 4.3, but that’s expected. You’re still on dialysis three times a week. The nephrology team increased your cinacalcet to 60 mg twice daily to help control your PTH and slow the calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they said I might need surgery on my parathyroid glands. Is that still the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Outpatient surgery is still recommended. We’ll follow up with the surgeon once you’re stable. For now, we’re focusing on infection control and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting ready to discharge you to the extended care facility. You’ll finish a 7-day course of oral clindamycin and ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to follow up with dermatology for the injections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We couldn’t schedule it yet, but if you don’t hear from them in two business days, call the clinic directly. Also, keep taking your oxycodone as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really want to switch dialysis centers. The one I’m at isn’t good to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noted that. The care team will help you explore other options. Your health and comfort matter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel a bit better. The pain isn’t gone, but it’s more manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Keep up with wound care, take your meds, and follow up with your doctors. You’re doing the right things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I do. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for worsening skin pain due to calciphylaxis, with concern for superimposed soft tissue infection. She presented with increased pain in wounds on her left hip, right breast, and abdomen after dialysis. Initial labs showed elevated WBC, and she was started on IV clindamycin and ciprofloxacin, later transitioned to oral therapy. Dermatology recommended intralesional sodium thiosulfate injections for outpatient management. The nephrology team increased cinacalcet to 60 mg BID to address elevated PTH contributing to calciphylaxis. The patient reported improved pain control with oxycodone and was willing to pursue injection therapy. She was discharged to an extended care facility to complete a 7-day antibiotic course, continue dialysis, and arrange follow-up with dermatology and surgery. Concerns about her current dialysis center were documented for care coordination.
